lines.orig: Seven TinyGPTs, from 8 thousand to 1.8 million parameters. Same data, same 3.1 million tokens each. Bigger models land lower, with smaller gains at the top.
lines.visuals: Real validation curves of 7 model sizes trained on the same 3,072,000 tokens: 8.4k params → 0.888, 22k params → 0.672, 36k params → 0.646, 171k params → 0.488, 478k params → 0.474, 834k params → 0.474, 1.8M params → 0.464.

lines.orig: Plot final loss against size on a log axis, and the dots fall on a smooth curve: a power law. Every time you multiply the size, the loss above a floor shrinks by a predictable factor. Here it flattens near 0.42, but only for this token budget: the same 171 thousand parameter model trained on four times more tokens reaches 0.45 instead of 0.49.
lines.visuals: Real final losses vs non-embedding parameters (log x) with the fitted power law L(N) = c + a·N^-α: a = 12.948, α = 0.408, c = 0.417 (R² = 0.989).

lines.orig: Now plot the same runs against compute. For a tiny budget, small models win. As the budget grows, the best choice keeps shifting to bigger models. Following the lower edge, the winner goes from 8 thousand to 1.8 million parameters.
lines.visuals: Real validation loss vs training FLOPs (log x; FLOPs = 6 × all params × tokens) for all 7 sizes; the thick gray line is the lower envelope (best loss at each budget, curves interpolated in log FLOPs). Winners along it, small to large budget: 8.4k → 22k → 36k → 171k → 478k → 834k → 1.8M. Caveat: intermediate checkpoints of fixed-length cosine runs.

lines.orig: Big labs found the same shape at vastly larger scale. Kaplan and colleagues, 2020: loss follows smooth power laws in parameters, data and compute. Then Chinchilla, 2022: for a fixed budget, grow the model and the training data together. Their 70 billion parameter model saw 1.4 trillion tokens, about 20 per parameter.
lines.visuals: Two cards. Kaplan et al. 2020: loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute over many orders of magnitude. Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla): at fixed compute, scale parameters and tokens in roughly equal proportion; Chinchilla = 70B params on 1.4T tokens (≈ 20 tokens per parameter).

lines.orig: By Chinchilla's rule of thumb, derived for huge web-text runs, our 4 biggest models would want more tokens: the largest saw just 1.7 per parameter. But our data repeats itself, so treat that as a rough guide. And real labs often train far past 20 tokens per parameter, to make models cheaper to run.
lines.visuals: Real tokens-per-parameter of each run (3,072,000 tokens / params): 8.4k: 364.3, 22k: 138.5, 36k: 86.0, 171k: 18.0, 478k: 6.4, 834k: 3.7, 1.8M: 1.7. A yellow dashed line marks Chinchilla's ≈ 20 tokens per parameter (a compute-optimal allocation heuristic for large web-text runs, not a 'trained enough' threshold). Our corpus is highly redundant: the 171k model reached val 0.491 on 256k tokens vs 0.488 on all of them.

lines.orig: For your own models: train a ladder of small ones first, fit the curve, and predict before you spend. Balance size and data for your budget, and remember where the curve flattens depends on the data. Our fit is seven tiny models, one seed, one learning rate: the shape, not a law.
lines.visuals: Takeaways: train a ladder of small models first; fit the curve, predict the big one; balance size and data for your budget; where the curve flattens depends on the data. Caveat: our fit uses 7 tiny models, one seed and one learning rate for every size.
